{
  "hook": "High-elevation fruit from Valle de Tupungato gives this Chardonnay a bright citrus backbone and a stony mineral bite. Multiple gold medals at Berliner and Asia Wine Trophy make it an easy sell on lists looking for crisp Argentine white at mid-market prices.",
  "wine_summary": "Valle de Tupungato sits on the eastern foothills of the Andes; that site imprint is the reason this Chardonnay matters — the fruit arrives with higher natural acidity and concentrated flavor because cool nights slow ripening. Atamisque's bottlings (noted across 2010, 2015, 2017, 2018 and NV vintages with repeated trophy recognition) deliver a restrained style that reads more Chablis than tropical Mendoza: citrus, green apple and a saline, talc-like mineral impression. The producer does not publish exhaustive cellar technicals for these releases, but consistent medal-level performance signals a repeatable house approach aimed at clarity rather than overt oak.",
  "terroir_expression": "Valle de Tupungato vineyards occupy high-altitude alluvial terraces and colluvial deposits derived from Andean fluvial and glacial processes; soils tend toward sand and gravel over a calcareous or silty sublayer. That free-draining, low-vigor mix forces vines to root deeply, concentrating acidity and producing wines with tight citrus tension and a crushed-stone minerality that shows as linearity on the palate.",
  "vinification_summary": "Atamisque does not widely publish detailed vinification for this line; tasting evidence—bright acidity, moderate texture, and limited vanilla—indicates predominant stainless-steel fermentation or aging in neutral oak, with malolactic fermentation either suppressed or used sparingly (malolactic converts apple-like malic acid into softer lactic acid, which would blunt the wine's crispness). That restraint preserves the site-driven citrus and mineral profile rather than producing buttery, tropical Chardonnay.",
  "food_pairing": "Nashville hot chicken with pickles — high acidity and mineral drive cut the fried heat and refresh the palate.\nSeared sea scallops with brown butter and lemon — the wine's citrus and saline notes balance the butter while lifting the shellfish flavor.\nRoasted halibut with a light beurre blanc and spring asparagus — acidity cleans the sauce and the wine's stony edge matches asparagus's green bitterness.\nGoat cheese tart (chevre and caramelized onion) — acidity contrasts the fattiness and the wine's mineral thread echoes the cheese's tang.",
  "comparable_wines": "Salentein Reserve Chardonnay — similar high-altitude Mendoza origin and a restrained oak program that emphasizes acidity and minerality.\nTrapiche Medalla Chardonnay — another Mendoza white at a comparable price point that balances fruit purity with modest oak influence.",
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry white with crisp acidity and pronounced mineral focus",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through year 6 from vintage for best fruit-acid balance; store at 10–13°C away from light and temperature swings.",
  "value_assessment": "Price: US$10–US$20. At that range it competes with Trapiche Medalla (US$12–16) and Salentein Reserve Chardonnay (US$14–20). It is worth buying if you want a high-altitude, acidity-driven Argentine Chardonnay that reads cool-climate rather than tropical—good score-to-price ratio for restaurants and retail.",
  "market_position": "This sits on lists and retail shelves aimed at diners and buyers who want a bright, food-friendly white without Champagne pricing; think bistro, seafood-focused restaurants, and specialty wine shops that feature Argentine regional expressions. Collectors are unlikely to prioritize it over top-tier single-vineyard Mendoza whites; its audience is practical buyers and sommeliers building mixed lists.",
  "insider_take": "If you expect a ripe, buttery Mendoza Chardonnay you will be disappointed; this is a tradeoff: restrained oak and lifted acidity instead of tropical ripeness and cream. Buy it if you want crisp, mineral-driven white for food matching; skip it if you want an oak-forward New World Chardonnay.",

parsed.hook: High-elevation fruit from Valle de Tupungato gives this Chardonnay a bright citrus backbone and a stony mineral bite. Multiple gold medals at Berliner and Asia Wine Trophy make it an easy sell on lists looking for crisp Argentine white at mid-market prices.
parsed.wine_summary: Valle de Tupungato sits on the eastern foothills of the Andes; that site imprint is the reason this Chardonnay matters — the fruit arrives with higher natural acidity and concentrated flavor because cool nights slow ripening. Atamisque's bottlings (noted across 2010, 2015, 2017, 2018 and NV vintages with repeated trophy recognition) deliver a restrained style that reads more Chablis than tropical Mendoza: citrus, green apple and a saline, talc-like mineral impression. The producer does not publish exhaustive cellar technicals for these releases, but consistent medal-level performance signals a repeatable house approach aimed at clarity rather than overt oak.
parsed.terroir_expression: Valle de Tupungato vineyards occupy high-altitude alluvial terraces and colluvial deposits derived from Andean fluvial and glacial processes; soils tend toward sand and gravel over a calcareous or silty sublayer. That free-draining, low-vigor mix forces vines to root deeply, concentrating acidity and producing wines with tight citrus tension and a crushed-stone minerality that shows as linearity on the palate.
parsed.vinification_summary: Atamisque does not widely publish detailed vinification for this line; tasting evidence—bright acidity, moderate texture, and limited vanilla—indicates predominant stainless-steel fermentation or aging in neutral oak, with malolactic fermentation either suppressed or used sparingly (malolactic converts apple-like malic acid into softer lactic acid, which would blunt the wine's crispness). That restraint preserves the site-driven citrus and mineral profile rather than producing buttery, tropical Chardonnay.
parsed.food_pairing:
Nashville hot chicken with pickles — high acidity and mineral drive cut the fried heat and refresh the palate.
Seared sea scallops with brown butter and lemon — the wine's citrus and saline notes balance the butter while lifting the shellfish flavor.
Roasted halibut with a light beurre blanc and spring asparagus — acidity cleans the sauce and the wine's stony edge matches asparagus's green bitterness.
Goat cheese tart (chevre and caramelized onion) — acidity contrasts the fattiness and the wine's mineral thread echoes the cheese's tang.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Salentein Reserve Chardonnay — similar high-altitude Mendoza origin and a restrained oak program that emphasizes acidity and minerality.
Trapiche Medalla Chardonnay — another Mendoza white at a comparable price point that balances fruit purity with modest oak influence.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-bodied dry white with crisp acidity and pronounced mineral focus
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through year 6 from vintage for best fruit-acid balance; store at 10–13°C away from light and temperature swings.
parsed.value_assessment: Price: US$10–US$20. At that range it competes with Trapiche Medalla (US$12–16) and Salentein Reserve Chardonnay (US$14–20). It is worth buying if you want a high-altitude, acidity-driven Argentine Chardonnay that reads cool-climate rather than tropical—good score-to-price ratio for restaurants and retail.
parsed.market_position: This sits on lists and retail shelves aimed at diners and buyers who want a bright, food-friendly white without Champagne pricing; think bistro, seafood-focused restaurants, and specialty wine shops that feature Argentine regional expressions. Collectors are unlikely to prioritize it over top-tier single-vineyard Mendoza whites; its audience is practical buyers and sommeliers building mixed lists.
parsed.insider_take: If you expect a ripe, buttery Mendoza Chardonnay you will be disappointed; this is a tradeoff: restrained oak and lifted acidity instead of tropical ripeness and cream. Buy it if you want crisp, mineral-driven white for food matching; skip it if you want an oak-forward New World Chardonnay.
